submission.natural_language_explanation: The negative pole fires on a moderately frequent family of common English words - everyday concrete/institutional nouns (group, class, team, school, hospital, church, laboratory, bank, factory, medicine, cells, tissue, blood, oxygen, skin, soil, stone, carpet, wall, roof, window, door, gate) and the generic degree/similarity words (such, so, most, especially, particularly, usually) - with mean strengths of 0.10-0.35 in natural prose, and it holds at a low floor everywhere else (median 0.02 over 85k scanned tokens, below the audit's active line on ~83% of them). It is near-silent (mean under 0.05) on abstract or taxonomic vocabulary (concept, idea, theory, system, method, process, structure, pattern, model, range) and on plural count quantifiers (many, several, various, few, multiple, numerous), weaker on nature/animal nouns (dog, tree, river, island, bird), and it is retrospective: the peak is a function of the token and its immediate context, not of surprisal or next-token entropy (correlations ~0) and not of any upcoming-token role (zero-ablation KL ~1e-5, far below the 1e-3 lookahead gate; the Jacobian lens is diffuse, kurtosis 3.3).

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
On the eastern edge of Marlow, where the old cattle market once stood, a long brick factory has been turned into a community centre. For most of the last century it made wool blankets, and the town's fortunes rose and fell with the mill. When the works closed, the site sat empty for nearly a decade. The roof sagged, the windows were boarded, and weeds pushed up through the stone floor.

I walked there last spring with Ada, who taught a history class at the secondary school for thirty years. She remembers the whistle that called the workers in at seven each morning, and the gate at the north end where the carts came through. 'There was a whole group of us who met by that gate,' she said. 'We would stand in the mud and talk about the weekend, then go in when the bell rang. My mother worked in the spinning room, and my aunt ran the canteen. Nobody had much, but the place felt like a second home.'

The restoration took four years and a great deal of argument. The council raised part of the money, a bank on the high street donated the rest, and the church across the road lent chairs for the first public meeting. Engineers from a laboratory at the county hospital tested the soil before the foundations were poured, because the dye works next door had left arsenic in the ground. They found traces in the top few inches and nothing deeper, which was a relief. The report said the risk to future visitors was low, though it advised keeping the beds along the south wall raised and covered.

Inside, the building has been left deliberately rough. The old carpet in the office has gone, the ceiling beams are exposed, and a long counter made of reclaimed timber runs the length of the hall. On the far side, behind a glass door, there is a small room of exhibits: wooden bobbins, a leather belt from the drive shaft, photographs of the annual outing to the coast. Ada pointed at one of them and laughed. 'That's me, second from the left, aged nineteen. I had no idea what I was doing.'

The centre now runs a nursery, a cafe, and evening classes in pottery and upholstery. There is a clinic on Thursdays and a job club on Mondays, and the upper floor has been let to a software firm whose staff, according to the manager, mostly work from home. On the day I visited, a team of volunteers was sorting donations in the yard: coats, saucepans, a bicycle with no saddle. Most of the stock goes to families who have recently arrived in the county, so the food bank has been busier than at any time in its history. One of the volunteers told me that the queue now starts before eight in the morning.

What strikes you, walking around, is how the building keeps its old shape. The walls still carry the marks of the machinery that was bolted to them. The windows are tall and narrow, so the light could reach the looms. The gate at the north end has been kept, though it no longer opens. Ada said the town had been slow to accept the change, and that such places usually are, but that the arguments faded once people saw children playing where the machines used to stand.

On my way out I stopped by the noticeboard. There were notices for a choir, a walking group, a first aid course, and a reminder that the museum would be closed on the bank holiday. The paper was curling at the corners, and someone had drawn a small dog in the margin. It seemed a hopeful sort of mess.
